notes.front: What do PromQL's topk and bottomk aggregation operators do?
notes.back: They return a subset of k elements from the input vector, keeping the original labels: topk the largest values, bottomk the smallest.
notes.explanation: Unlike other aggregators, they return actual vector elements rather than a single aggregated value, so the source series stay identifiable.
notes.example: Like picking the 5 tallest people from a crowd and keeping their name tags on, rather than just reporting the group's average height.

notes.front: What does the count_values(l, v) aggregation operator do?
notes.back: One series per unique sample value in v, labelled l with that value; each series' value is how often it occurred.
notes.explanation: It's the aggregation to reach for when the thing you want to count is a value itself, rather than a label.
notes.example: Like tallying how many students got each exam score, rather than each student's own score.

notes.front: What does the quantile(φ, v) aggregation operator calculate?
notes.back: The φ-quantile (0 ≤ φ ≤ 1) over the dimensions being aggregated, the value that ranks at number φ×N among the N input values.
notes.explanation: It works only on float samples in the input vector, quite unlike histogram_quantile, which reads bucketed histogram data instead.
notes.example: Like reading off the value at the 95th mark once N measurements are lined up smallest to largest.

notes.front: What is vector matching in PromQL?
notes.back: How a binary operator finds a matching element in the right-hand vector for each entry in the left-hand vector, when operating between two instant vectors.
notes.explanation: Without a match, an entry from one side simply has nothing to combine with, so it drops out of the result by default.
notes.example: Like matching up left and right shoes from two separate piles: only pairs that share the same size and style get matched.

notes.front: What is one-to-one vector matching?
notes.back: The default matching behaviour: each left-hand entry finds a unique pair on the right, matched by an identical label set.
notes.explanation: It's the plain case of `vector1 <operator> vector2`, before `on`, `ignoring`, `group_left` or `group_right` reshape how matching happens.
notes.example: Like pairing each guest at a dinner with exactly one place setting: one guest, one seat.

notes.front: What do the group_left and group_right modifiers do in PromQL?
notes.back: They enable many-to-one or one-to-many vector matching, letting one element on the "one" side match several on the "many" side.
notes.explanation: left/right names which side of the operator has the higher cardinality: group_left means the left vector does, group_right means the right vector does.
notes.example: Like matching one team captain (the "one" side) against every player on their team (the "many" side).
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Operators, "Many-to-one and one-to-many vector matches"

notes.front: What do label_replace() and label_join() do?
notes.back: label_replace sets a destination label from a regular-expression match on a source label; label_join joins several labels' values into one, with a separator.
notes.explanation: Both act on float and histogram samples in the same way, and label_replace returns a series unchanged if its regular expression doesn’t match.
notes.example: Like relabelling one shipping box from a barcode already stuck to it, or combining a box's aisle and shelf codes into one location code.

notes.front: What does the histogram_quantile() function do?
notes.back: It calculates the φ-quantile (0 ≤ φ ≤ 1) of observations from a classic histogram's buckets, or from a native histogram sample.
notes.explanation: It's the function that turns a histogram's raw bucket counts into an actual quantile value, such as a 90th-percentile request duration.
notes.example: Like reading a percentile off a bucketed survey of exam scores, rather than being told the percentile directly.

notes.front: What is a native histogram?
notes.back: A histogram exposed and ingested as one composite sample per timestamp, holding the count and sum of observations together with a dynamic set of buckets.
notes.explanation: That's the contrast with a classic histogram, which spreads the same information across several separate float series instead of one composite sample.
notes.example: Like one parcel holding a whole itemised receipt, instead of a separate slip of paper for every line item.

notes.front: What are native histograms with custom bucket boundaries (NHCB)?
notes.back: A form of native histogram that Prometheus can ingest classic histograms into, keeping the classic histogram's own configured bucket layout.
notes.explanation: They're a middle ground: stored efficiently like other native histograms, but still limited by the same fixed bucket boundaries a classic histogram was instrumented with.
notes.example: Like repacking the same fixed-size crates into one efficient container, without changing the size of the crates themselves.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Histograms and summaries, "Instrumentation library support"

notes.front: What is a recording rule?
notes.back: A rule that precomputes a frequently needed or expensive PromQL expression and saves its result as a new set of time series.
notes.explanation: Querying the saved result is then often much faster than re-running the original expression, which matters most for dashboards that re-query it on every refresh.
notes.example: Like precooking a dish that's ordered constantly, rather than cooking it fresh from scratch every single time it's requested.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Defining recording rules, "Recording rules"

notes.front: What does sum(v) calculate in PromQL?
notes.back: The sum of the sample values in v, applied the same way the + binary operator adds two values.
notes.explanation: Mixing float samples and histogram samples in one sum is invalid, and the affected element is dropped from the result with a warning.

notes.front: avg(v) divides the sum of v by the {{c1::number of aggregated samples}}, the same way the / binary operator does.
notes.explanation: So avg is really sum followed by a division, and it inherits the same rule against mixing float and histogram samples.

notes.front: Do min(v) and max(v) operate on histogram samples in the input vector?
notes.back: No. They only work on float samples; histogram samples are ignored, flagged by an info-level annotation.
notes.explanation: That's a narrower behaviour than sum or avg, which do accept histogram samples, provided none are mixed with floats.

notes.front: group(v) returns {{c1::1}} for each group that contains any value at that timestamp.
notes.explanation: The values being grouped may be float or histogram samples.

notes.front: What does count(v) return?
notes.back: The number of values present at that timestamp, or no value at all if none are present.
notes.explanation: Unlike min, max, stddev and stdvar, count accepts both float and histogram samples in v.

notes.front: Do stddev(v) and stdvar(v) work on histogram samples?
notes.back: No. Both only work with float samples; histogram samples in the input vector are ignored, flagged by an info-level annotation.
notes.explanation: stddev returns the standard deviation of v and stdvar its variance, and both follow this same restriction to floats.

notes.front: What's the difference between a by clause and a without clause on an aggregation operator?
notes.back: by keeps only the listed labels in the result, dropping everything else. without removes the listed labels, keeping all the rest.
notes.explanation: So the two clauses are opposites of each other over the same label list, and picking the wrong one silently changes what the result is grouped by.
notes.contrast: by (application, group) keeps just those two labels; without (instance) drops only instance and keeps everything else, including application and group.

notes.front: A dashboard should show the 5 instances currently consuming the most memory, keeping each instance's own labels visible. Which aggregation operator fits: topk or sum?
notes.back: topk(5, memory_consumption_bytes). sum would collapse the instances into one number, losing exactly the labels the dashboard needs.
notes.explanation: topk and bottomk are the operators built to return a subset of the original elements, with their labels intact, rather than one aggregated value.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Operators, "topk and bottomk", example

notes.front: In an instant query, how are the series returned by topk and bottomk ordered?
notes.back: By value, descending for topk and ascending for bottomk, with NaN treated as farthest from the top or bottom respectively.
notes.explanation: That ordering guarantee holds for instant queries; no sorting applies to range queries.

notes.front: A team wants to know how many running binaries report each build_version value. Which aggregation operator, applied to the build_version metric, answers this directly?
notes.back: count_values, e.g. count_values("version", build_version): one series per version, valued at how many binaries report it.
notes.explanation: This is exactly the operator's own worked example: counting binaries by the version value they report.

notes.front: Does the quantile(φ, v) aggregation operator work on histogram samples in v?
notes.back: No. It only works with float samples; histogram samples in the input vector are ignored, flagged by an info-level annotation.
notes.explanation: For φ = NaN, NaN is returned; for φ < 0, -Inf; for φ > 1, +Inf.

notes.front: What are two of the six binary arithmetic operators PromQL supports?
notes.back: Any two of: + (addition), - (subtraction), * (multiplication), / (division), % (modulo), ^ (power).
notes.explanation: They follow IEEE 754 floating-point arithmetic, including its handling of special values such as NaN, +Inf and -Inf.

notes.front: Between two histogram samples, which arithmetic operators are valid?
notes.back: Only + and -. Each adds or subtracts all matching bucket populations and the count and sum of observations.
notes.explanation: Every other arithmetic operator between two histogram samples removes that element from the result, flagged by an info-level annotation.

notes.front: For a histogram sample divided by a scalar (/), the docs say the histogram must be on which side of the operator?
notes.back: The left-hand side, with the scalar on the right. Every bucket population, count and sum is then divided by the scalar.
notes.explanation: Between a scalar and a histogram sample only two operations work: * (every bucket population, count and sum multiplied) and / with the histogram on the left. Any other combination, including + and -, removes that element from the result.

notes.front: What happens to the metric name in any arithmetic binary operation involving vectors?
notes.back: It is dropped, even if __name__ was explicitly named in an on clause.
notes.explanation: Comparison operators differ: without bool they keep the left side’s metric name, with some exceptions.

notes.front: What are two of the six binary comparison operators PromQL supports?
notes.back: Any two of: == (equal), != (not-equal), > (greater-than), < (less-than), >= (greater-or-equal), <= (less-or-equal).
notes.explanation: They're defined between scalar/scalar, vector/scalar and vector/vector value pairs.

notes.front: By default, what do PromQL's comparison operators do to a vector, rather than returning true/false values?
notes.back: They filter it: elements where the comparison is false, or which find no match, are dropped from the result vector.
notes.explanation: This default behaviour is why up == 0 returns only the down targets, not a 0/1 value for every target.

notes.front: Adding the {{c1::bool}} modifier after a comparison operator makes it return 0 or 1 for the value, instead of filtering.
notes.explanation: Between two scalars, this modifier isn't optional: bool must be provided for a comparison to return a scalar result at all.

notes.front: You want every target's up value shown as 0 or 1, rather than having down targets dropped from the result. Which modifier do you add to up == 1?
notes.back: bool, written as up == bool 1. This returns 1 or 0 for every matched target instead of filtering any out.
notes.explanation: Without bool, the comparison would drop every target that fails the check, leaving only the up ones.

notes.front: vector1 and vector2 results in the elements of vector1 for which vector2 has {{c1::exactly matching label sets}}; the rest are dropped.
notes.explanation: The metric name and values it keeps are carried over from vector1, never from vector2.

notes.front: What does vector1 or vector2 return?
notes.back: All of vector1's elements, plus every element of vector2 that has no matching label set already in vector1.
notes.explanation: So vector1's elements always win on overlap; vector2 only contributes what vector1 doesn't already have.

notes.front: What does vector1 unless vector2 return?
notes.back: The elements of vector1 that have no exactly matching label set in vector2; any matching elements in both are dropped.
notes.explanation: It's the complement of and: and keeps the overlap, unless keeps everything except the overlap.

notes.front: What's the difference between the on and ignoring vector matching keywords?
notes.back: on(labels) matches only on the listed labels. ignoring(labels) matches on every label except the listed ones.
notes.explanation: Both reshape which labels two vectors are matched on, in opposite directions, much like by and without do for aggregation.
notes.contrast: on(code) matches purely by the code label; ignoring(code) matches on every other shared label and disregards code.

notes.front: method_code:http_errors:rate5m has a code label; method:http_requests:rate5m does not. To divide error rate by request rate per method, what keyword lets the two vectors match despite that difference?
notes.back: ignoring(code), as in method_code:http_errors:rate5m{code="500"} / ignoring(code) method:http_requests:rate5m.
notes.explanation: Without ignoring(code), no pair would share an identical label set, so the division would return nothing at all.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Operators, "One-to-one vector matches", example

notes.front: method_code:http_errors:rate5m has several entries per method (split further by code), while method:http_requests:rate5m has just one entry per method. Dividing the two needs which modifier: group_left or group_right?
notes.back: group_left, because the left-hand vector (the errors, with the extra code label) is the side with higher cardinality.
notes.explanation: group_left allows many-to-one matching, where the left vector is the "many" side and the right vector is the "one" side.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Operators, "Many-to-one and one-to-many vector matches", example

notes.front: In a comparison binary operation without the bool modifier, which side's metric name is kept if group_right is used?
notes.back: The right side's metric name, to avoid collisions.
notes.explanation: Without group_right, the left side's metric name is normally the one kept, unless on is also used, which drops it entirely.

notes.front: Between an instant vector and a scalar, an arithmetic operator is applied to {{c1::the value of every data sample in the vector}}.
notes.explanation: So multiplying an instant vector of floats by 2 multiplies every sample's value by 2. As in any arithmetic operation involving vectors, the metric name is dropped from the result.

notes.front: In PromQL's binary operator precedence, which group of operators binds more tightly: * / % atan2, or + -?
notes.back: * / % atan2 bind more tightly than + -, which in turn bind more tightly than the comparison operators.
notes.explanation: ^ binds tightest of all and, unlike the others, is right-associative, so 2^3^2 is 2^(3^2), not (2^3)^2.

notes.front: A series carries service="a:c", and you want a new foo label holding just the part before the colon. Which function, and roughly how, gets you foo="a"?
notes.back: label_replace, matching a regex against service and capturing the part before the colon into $1, e.g. label_replace(v, "foo", "$1", "service", "(.*):.*").
notes.explanation: If the regular expression doesn't match a given series, that series is returned unchanged rather than erroring.

notes.front: A series has src1="a", src2="b" and src3="c", and you want one foo label holding "a,b,c". Which function does this, and with what separator argument?
notes.back: label_join, with "," as the separator: label_join(v, "foo", ",", "src1", "src2", "src3").
notes.explanation: label_join can join any number of source labels, unlike label_replace, which works from a single source label.

notes.front: A classic histogram with base name <basename> results in which three kinds of time series?
notes.back: <basename>_bucket{le="..."} for each bucket, <basename>_sum for the total of observed values, and <basename>_count for the number observed.
notes.explanation: <basename>_count is identical to <basename>_bucket{le="+Inf"}, since the +Inf bucket by definition contains every observation.

notes.front: If a classic histogram's configured bucket boundary has received no observations at all, does Prometheus still expose its _bucket series?
notes.back: Yes. Every configured bucket creates a _bucket series, whether or not it is populated.
notes.explanation: This "one series per bucket, populated or not" cost is exactly what makes classic histograms more expensive to store than NHCBs.

notes.front: A classic histogram's buckets are cumulative: every bucket counts all observations {{c1::less than or equal to its own upper boundary}}.
notes.explanation: That's what the le ("less or equal") label name on each bucket series stands for.

notes.front: For a classic histogram's cumulative buckets, what should be true of the bucket counts as le increases from one boundary to the next?
notes.back: They should be monotonically increasing (non-decreasing): a higher-le bucket's count can never be lower than a lower-le bucket's.
notes.explanation: That follows directly from cumulation: a bucket with a higher boundary contains every observation the lower one does, plus possibly more.

image.alt: Bar chart of a classic histogram's cumulative bucket counts for http_request_duration_seconds_bucket: le="0.1" holds 12, le="0.3" holds 30, le="1" holds 41, le="+Inf" holds 45. Each bar's count includes every observation at or below its own le boundary, so the counts only grow as le increases.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from Prometheus documentation, Metric types and Functions

notes.front: How do you calculate the 90th percentile of request durations over the last 10m from a classic histogram called http_request_duration_seconds?
notes.back: histogram_quantile(0.9, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[10m])).
notes.explanation: rate() is applied first to the raw bucket counters to get a per-second rate before histogram_quantile reads them.

notes.front: The same 90th-percentile query, but http_request_duration_seconds is now a native histogram. How does the expression change?
notes.back: histogram_quantile(0.9, rate(http_request_duration_seconds[10m])) — the same metric name, with no _bucket suffix needed.
notes.explanation: Native histogram samples carry their own buckets inside one composite sample, so there's no separate _bucket series to name.

notes.front: To aggregate a classic histogram's 90th percentile by job across all instances, which label must the by clause include alongside job, and why?
notes.back: le. histogram_quantile needs the le label present to read the buckets, so a by clause that drops it breaks the calculation.
notes.explanation: The full expression is histogram_quantile(0.9, sum by (job, le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[10m]))).

notes.front: For a classic histogram, what does histogram_quantile() return if b contains fewer than two buckets, and what must the highest bucket's upper bound be?
notes.back: It returns NaN with fewer than two buckets. The highest bucket must have an upper bound of +Inf, or NaN is returned as well.
notes.explanation: Both checks guard against a histogram that's missing the structure histogram_quantile needs to interpolate a value at all.

notes.front: How can histogram_quantile() be used to get the estimated minimum and maximum values stored in a histogram?
notes.back: histogram_quantile(0, v) for the estimated minimum, histogram_quantile(1, v) for the estimated maximum.
notes.explanation: These are just the φ=0 and φ=1 edges of the same quantile calculation, not a separate function.

notes.front: How do you calculate the average request duration over the last 5m from a classic histogram or summary called http_request_duration_seconds?
notes.back: rate(http_request_duration_seconds_sum[5m]) / rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[5m]).
notes.explanation: The count series behaves like a counter of requests, so dividing the rate of the sum by the rate of the count gives an average per observation.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Histograms and summaries, "Count and sum of observations"

notes.front: What's the equivalent average-duration expression for a native histogram, using histogram_sum and histogram_count?
notes.back: histogram_sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds[5m])) / histogram_count(rate(http_request_duration_seconds[5m])).
notes.explanation: A shorter equivalent also exists: histogram_avg(rate(http_request_duration_seconds[5m])).
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Histograms and summaries, "Count and sum of observations"

notes.front: The key property of a counter in Prometheus is that it always goes up, unless there is a counter reset, and the _count series of a summary or classic histogram {{c1::behaves exactly like a counter}}.
notes.explanation: That's why rate() is applied to _count the same way it would be applied to a metric named http_requests_total.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Histograms and summaries, "Count and sum of observations"

notes.front: What's the essential difference between how a summary and a histogram produce a quantile?
notes.back: A summary calculates streaming quantiles inside the instrumented program itself. A histogram exposes bucketed counts, and Prometheus calculates the quantile from those buckets.
notes.explanation: That difference is also why a histogram's quantile and time window can be changed at query time, while a summary's are fixed at instrumentation time.
notes.contrast: Summary: pre-calculated φ-quantiles chosen up front, expensive to record, not aggregatable. Histogram: bucketed counts, cheap to record, quantile computed ad hoc, aggregatable.

notes.front: A service runs several replicated instances, each exposing its own 95th-percentile summary. Does averaging those per-instance quantiles give a statistically valid overall 95th percentile?
notes.back: No. Aggregating a summary’s precomputed quantiles rarely makes sense, and here averaging them yields statistically nonsensical values.
notes.explanation: With histograms the docs sum the bucket rates across instances first, then histogram_quantile() computes one overall 95th percentile.

notes.front: For a classic histogram, what limits the error in a quantile that histogram_quantile() estimates?
notes.back: The width of the bucket the quantile value falls into: a wider bucket means a larger possible error.
notes.explanation: For a native histogram, the error is limited by the configured resolution instead, which is generally easier to tighten than redesigning a fixed classic bucket layout.

notes.front: With a target duration of 300ms and a tolerated duration of 1.2s, how is an Apdex score built from a native histogram's histogram_fraction()?
notes.back: The fraction of requests within the target, plus half the fraction between the target and the tolerated duration.
notes.explanation: The tolerated duration is usually 4 times the target duration, though this expression takes both as already-chosen values.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Histograms and summaries, "Apdex score"

notes.front: What's the main structural difference between a classic histogram and a native histogram in storage?
notes.back: Classic: several separate float series (_bucket, _sum, _count). Native: one composite sample per timestamp, holding buckets, sum and count together.
notes.explanation: In the TSDB, one native histogram is one time series of composite samples rather than a bunch of independent time series.
notes.contrast: Classic: many series, fixed bucket boundaries set at instrumentation time. Native: one series, dynamic exponential buckets at a configured resolution.

notes.front: An instrumentation library only supports classic histograms, but the team still wants more efficient storage. Can Prometheus still give them some of native histograms’ benefits, without changing the instrumentation?
notes.back: Yes, by configuring Prometheus to ingest the classic histogram as an NHCB, though it keeps the same fixed bucket layout and its limitations.
notes.explanation: NHCBs are only created on the Prometheus server side; on the instrumentation side, the metric still behaves exactly like a classic histogram.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Histograms and summaries, "Instrumentation library support"

notes.front: For a native histogram, what do histogram_count() and histogram_sum() return?
notes.back: histogram_count returns the number of observations stored in the histogram sample; histogram_sum returns the sum of the observed values.
notes.explanation: They give direct access to the two pieces a classic histogram would otherwise expose as separate _count and _sum series.

notes.front: histogram_avg(rate(http_request_duration_seconds[5m])) is a shorter equivalent of dividing {{c1::histogram_sum}} by histogram_count of the same rate expression.
notes.explanation: It exists purely as a convenience: it computes exactly the same average, without writing the division out.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Histograms and summaries, "Count and sum of observations"

notes.front: How do you calculate, from a native histogram, the fraction of HTTP requests over the last hour that took 200ms or less?
notes.back: histogram_fraction(0, 0.2, rate(http_request_duration_seconds[1h])).
notes.explanation: If the 0 and 0.2 boundaries don't land exactly on bucket edges, the function estimates the fraction by interpolation.

notes.front: Recording rules should be named in the general form {{c1::level:metric:operations}}.
notes.explanation: level is the aggregation level and labels of the rule's output, metric is the (largely unchanged) source metric name, and operations lists what was applied, newest first.

notes.front: A recording rule takes the rate() of requests_total over 5m for one instance and path. Following level:metric:operations, what would a sensible rule name be?
notes.back: instance_path:requests:rate5m — level names the labels kept (instance, path), metric drops _total, and operations records rate5m.
notes.explanation: That’s the docs’ own worked example: the naming convention strips _total off a counter’s name when rate() or irate() is used.

notes.front: When aggregating a ratio (such as a failure rate) up to a coarser level, what does the docs' guidance say to do, and what should you avoid?
notes.back: Aggregate the numerator and the denominator separately, then divide. Avoid taking the average of a ratio, or the average of an average.
notes.explanation: Averaging ratios directly isn't statistically valid, in the same way averaging summary quantiles isn't.

notes.front: instance_path:request_failures:rate5m and instance_path:requests:rate5m both exist per instance and path. To get the job-level failure ratio, aggregating away instance and path, what's the correct order of operations?
notes.back: sum without (instance, path) each of the two series first, then divide the summed failures by the summed requests.
notes.explanation: Dividing at the instance/path level first, then averaging those ratios, would give a statistically invalid result instead.

notes.front: When writing a recording rule, why does the docs' guidance say to always specify a without clause naming the labels being aggregated away?
notes.back: To preserve all the other labels, such as job, which avoids conflicts and gives more useful metrics and alerts.
notes.explanation: Leaving the without clause implicit risks silently dropping labels the rule's consumers still need.

notes.front: What must a recording rule's record field, the name of the series it writes, be?
notes.back: A valid metric name, following the same rules as any other Prometheus metric name.
notes.explanation: This is what lets a recording rule's output be queried later exactly like any other metric.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Defining recording rules, "Recording rules"

notes.front: A dashboard re-runs the same expensive aggregation over thousands of series on every refresh, making it slow to load. What's the fix, using what this topic teaches?
notes.back: Precompute that expression as a recording rule, and have the dashboard query the saved result instead of the original expression.
notes.explanation: Querying a recording rule's precomputed series is often much faster than re-running the original expression each time it's needed.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Defining recording rules, "Recording rules"

notes.front: memory_consumption_bytes has application, instance and group labels. You want total memory consumption per application and group, across all instances. Which expression does this?
notes.back: sum without (instance) (memory_consumption_bytes), equivalent to sum by (application, group) (memory_consumption_bytes).
notes.explanation: sum(v) adds up sample values the same way the + operator does between two values, here collapsing just the instance dimension away.

notes.front: You want only the targets that are currently down, using the up metric, not a 0/1 value for every target. Which comparison expression, with or without bool, gets this?
notes.back: up == 0, without bool. By default, comparison operators filter, dropping elements where the comparison is false or unmatched.
notes.explanation: Adding bool here would instead keep every target and turn the result into 0s and 1s, which isn't what's wanted for this particular query.

notes.front: You want the instances present in up_targets that are NOT present in maintenance_targets, dropping any that match on both sides. Which logical/set operator does this?
notes.back: unless: up_targets unless maintenance_targets keeps only up_targets elements with no exactly matching label set in maintenance_targets.
notes.explanation: and would instead keep only the overlap between the two vectors, the opposite of what's wanted here.

notes.front: An instant vector of byte counts needs converting to kilobytes for a graph. What does bytes_metric / 1024 do to the vector, label-wise?
notes.back: Every sample's value is divided by 1024; the other labels stay, but the metric name is dropped.
notes.explanation: That's the general rule for a vector combined with a scalar: the operator is applied to the value of every sample in the vector.

notes.front: A histogram is named http_request_duration_seconds. What is the exact series name for its count of observations at or below 0.5 seconds?
notes.back: http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.5"}.
notes.explanation: The same base name also produces _sum for the total of observed values and _count for the number observed.

notes.front: A histogram's le="0.1" bucket reports 30 observations and its le="0.3" bucket reports 24. Is this a valid cumulative bucket layout?
notes.back: No. Cumulative bucket counts must be monotonically increasing as le rises, so a higher-le bucket can never report fewer observations than a lower one.
notes.explanation: A le="0.3" bucket, having a higher boundary, must contain every observation the le="0.1" bucket does, plus possibly more.
